name: Cinnamon
lede: Cinnamon is the warm yellowish brown of the spice's bark, a color name that jewelers and pigment makers borrowed as well.

sections.title: The spice's color
sections.body: Paterson defines cinnamon as the yellowish brown of the spice, sometimes reddish or greyish and tinged with red [1]. As a color word it also grades diamonds: deep brown diamonds of little value are called cinnamon [1]. Our swatch is the Ridgway 1912 color (plate XXIX), also listed in ISCC-NBS (block 57) and in Maerz and Paul, who date the name to 1679 [2]. The xkcd survey's cinnamon is a much deeper burnt orange-brown, #AC4F06 [2]. Compare [[tawny]], [[adobe]], [[raw-umber]] and [[brown]].

sections.title: Cinnamon stone
sections.body: Jewelers use the name for essonite, also called hessonite, a reddish-yellow garnet that comes mostly from Sri Lanka [3]. It is sometimes confused with zircon [3]. The stone borrows its color word from the spice; see [[gem:garnet|garnet]].

sections.title: In the paint box and the vat
sections.body: Salter's 1869 account of cadmium brown describes a cinnamon-brown oxide, made by heating white cadmium carbonate [4]. It was unstable and said to revert quickly to white cadmium oxide [4]. Catechu, a dye extract sold in small cubes, is dark red-brown outside and a pale cinnamon-brown inside [5].

sections.title: On cloth
sections.body: In a spinning lesson Finlay watched, one basket held cinnamon-coloured cotton and another white, both bursting from brown husks [6]. A V&A monograph lists cinnamon among the colors of a textile fragment with yellow tulips, alongside peony red and verdigris [7]. The spice itself came with a price: medieval merchants from Venice held the spice monopoly and could inflate prices, even as cooks used cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon from the Indies in large quantities [8].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 1,070 (4.5%) hold this swatch within six units of ΔE2000 over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [9]. India leads: 107 of 721 paintings (14.8%, 3.3 times the average) [9]. Among movements, Mughal paintings match in 34 of 168 (20.2%, 4.5 times) and Rajput paintings in 16 of 97 (16.5%) [9].

In time it is strongest in the 1300s, at 2.3 times the average, and weakest in the 1600s, at 0.76 [9]. In 82% of its paintings it is a highlight, the lightest part of the palette [9]. The strongest match is Hua Ziyou's *Bathing of the Buddha Festival*, 1833, where it covers 66% of the picture [9]. We have not checked whether such matches are a pigment, a paper or a silk ground, and these are photographs of aged, varnished paintings: a color match, not a pigment test. See [[painting:aic-80720|Bathing of the Buddha Festival]].
